html:
The Ghana Empire, called Wagadu by its own people, was a kingdom of the western Sahel, in what is now southeastern Mauritania and western Mali. It grew rich on the gold trade across the Sahara and lasted from at least the 8th century, possibly much earlier, until the 13th.

Its people were the Soninke. "Ghana" was the title of the king, which Arab writers used as the name of the country. When it began is unknown; the first written mention comes from the Baghdad scholar al-Khwarizmi around 830, and its origins may go back to about 300.

Its wealth came from its place in the trans-Saharan trade. Ghana sat between the gold fields to the south and the caravan routes to the north. It did not mine the gold but controlled and taxed its passage: the king kept all gold nuggets for himself and left the gold dust for trade.

The best account comes from the Andalusian geographer al-Bakri, writing in 1068. He describes a capital of two towns: one for Muslim merchants, with twelve mosques, and one for the king, who kept his own religion while employing Muslims as officials. The ruins at Koumbi Saleh in Mauritania are thought to be the merchants' town.

The old story that the Almoravids conquered Ghana in 1076 is now doubted by many historians. More likely the empire was weakened by drought, shifting trade routes and new rivals. By the 13th century it had become a vassal of the rising Mali Empire under Sundiata Keita.

When the Gold Coast won independence in 1957, Kwame Nkrumah named it Ghana after the old empire, although the two do not overlap on the map.
